p: Good evening, my dear friend. Last time we watched the gradients of chords settle towards two, as the second point crept towards the first. Tonight we look hard at that word, settle. It is called a limit, and it is the foundation stone of the summit. It took mathematicians a hundred and fifty years after Newton to lay it properly, so if it feels slippery at first, you are in excellent company.
## Closer and closer

Consider the numbers one, a half, a third, a quarter, a fifth, and so on: one over n, as n grows. They get smaller and smaller, closer and closer to nought, though none of them is ever nought. We say the limit of one over n, as n tends to infinity, is nought.
$$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}=0
In plain words: the limit, as n tends to infinity, of one over n, equals nought.
The important point is this. The limit is not reached. It is the value the sequence gets as close to as you please, and stays close to, if you go far enough.
?? While I pour. What is the limit of one plus one over n, as n tends to infinity?
=> One. The one over n part shrinks to nought, leaving one.
## Achilles and the tortoise

Zeno of Elea, about four hundred and fifty years before Christ, told of swift Achilles racing a tortoise with a head start. By the time Achilles reaches where the tortoise was, it has moved on a little. By the time he reaches that point, it has moved on again. And so on, for ever. So, said Zeno, Achilles can never catch it.

The resolution is a limit. Suppose Achilles runs ten times as fast, and the tortoise starts a hundred yards ahead. Achilles runs a hundred yards, then ten, then one, then a tenth, and so on. The total distance, a hundred and eleven point one one one and so on, settles towards a hundred and eleven and one ninth yards. Infinitely many stages, but a finite total distance, and a finite time. At that point, he passes the tortoise.
## The value at the point need not matter

Here is the key to calculus. Consider the expression x squared minus one, over x minus one. What happens near x equals one? At exactly one, it is nought over nought, which is meaningless. But try nearby values. At one point one, it is two point one. At one point nought one, two point nought one. At nought point nine nine, one point nine nine. It settles towards two.

Algebra shows why. The top factorises as, x minus one, times, x plus one. For any x other than one, the x minus one cancels, leaving x plus one, which is near two when x is near one. The expression has a hole at x equals one, but the limit fills it.
That is exactly the situation with the gradient of a tangent: rise over run, both shrinking to nought, but the ratio settling to a definite value.
?? What is the limit, as x tends to two, of x squared minus four, over x minus two?
=> The top is, x minus two, times, x plus two. Cancel, leaving x plus two, which tends to four.
## The scandal of the infinitesimal

Newton and Leibniz did not use limits in this careful way. They spoke of quantities that were infinitely small but not quite nought, called infinitesimals, or of ultimate ratios of vanishing quantities. They divided by them as if they were something, and then threw them away as if they were nothing. It worked magnificently, but it troubled thoughtful people.

In 1734 Bishop George Berkeley published a pamphlet called The Analyst, mocking the infinitesimals as the ghosts of departed quantities. He had a point. For over a century the calculus produced right answers on shaky foundations.
## Cauchy and Weierstrass

In my own century the foundations were repaired. Augustin-Louis Cauchy, in Paris, in his lectures published in the 1820s, built calculus on limits. Karl Weierstrass, in Berlin, made the definition fully precise around the middle of the century. His definition says, in words: the limit is L if you can make the quantity as close to L as anyone demands, by taking the variable close enough to its target. A game: you name how close you want to be; I show how near I must go to guarantee it. If I can always win, the limit exists.
The ghosts were laid to rest. Calculus stood on solid rock.
## Summary

A limit is the value a quantity settles towards, made as close as we please by going far enough or near enough, whether or not it ever arrives. Limits explain Zeno's Achilles and give meaning to nought over nought, as in the gradient of a tangent. Berkeley mocked the old infinitesimals in 1734; Cauchy and Weierstrass made limits rigorous in the nineteenth century. Next, the derivative. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Two lectures ago we crept along a curve with chords. Last time we learnt what a limit is. Tonight we put the two together and define the central object of the first half of calculus: the derivative. Once it is defined, I promise, there are rules that make it quick to find, and next time we shall use them.
## The recipe, in words

Choose a point on the curve, at x. Take a tiny step to the right, of size h. The height goes from f of x to f of x plus h. The chord between the two points has a rise of f of x plus h minus f of x, and a run of h. Its gradient is the rise over the run. Now let h shrink to nought, and take the limit. That limit is the derivative.
$$ f'(x)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
In plain words: f prime of x, which the British often call f dash, the derivative, is the limit, as h tends to nought, of, f of x plus h, minus f of x, all over h.
Read it as: the rise, over a tiny run, as the run vanishes.
## Working it out for x squared
Let f of x be x squared. Then f of x plus h is, x plus h, all squared, which expands, as we learnt with brackets, to x squared plus two x h plus h squared.
Take away f of x, which is x squared. The x squared vanishes, leaving two x h plus h squared.
Divide by h: two x plus h.
Now let h shrink to nought. Two x plus h becomes two x.
$$ \frac{d}{dx}x^{2}=2x
In plain words: the derivative of x squared is two x.

Check with last time: at x equals one, two x is two. Exactly what the chords were settling towards. And notice: the formula gives the gradient at every point at once. At x equals three, the gradient is six; at x equals minus two, it is minus four, sloping downhill, as the left arm of the U should; at nought, it is nought, level at the bottom.
?? While I pour. Using the derivative two x, what is the gradient of y equals x squared at x equals five?
=> Two times five, ten.
## Three notations

Here the old quarrel shows itself in our symbols. Leibniz wrote d y by d x: a tiny change in y over a tiny change in x. It looks like a fraction, and often behaves like one, which is why it is so useful.
$$ \frac{dy}{dx}

Newton put a dot over the letter, y dot, for the rate of change in time. Physicists still use his dot for velocity. And Joseph-Louis Lagrange, in 1797, introduced f dash of x, sometimes called f prime of x, and the word derivative itself comes from his French, fonction dérivée. All three mean the same thing. I shall mostly use Leibniz's, partly because it is so expressive and partly to annoy my umbrella Newton.
## Speed

If s is the distance travelled after time t, then d s by d t is the speed at that instant. Galileo found that a dropped stone falls about sixteen times t squared feet in t seconds. The derivative of sixteen t squared is thirty-two t. So after one second, it falls at thirty-two feet per second; after two seconds, sixty-four. The speed grows steadily by thirty-two feet per second, every second. That steady growth is the acceleration due to gravity, which you may have heard as about thirty-two feet per second per second, or nine point eight metres.
?? How fast is the stone falling after three seconds?
=> Thirty-two times three, ninety-six feet per second.
## The derivative is a new function

The derivative of a function is another function. From x squared, the derivative machine produces two x. Feed in a function, out comes its rate-of-change function. Picture it as a graph drawn beneath the first: where the original graph rises, the derivative is above the axis; where it falls, below; where it is level, at a peak or a valley, the derivative is exactly nought. That last fact will let us find highest and lowest points, in a lecture to come.
## When there is no derivative

Not every function has a derivative everywhere. A graph with a sharp corner, like a letter V, has no single tangent at the corner: approaching from the left, the slope is one thing; from the right, another. The limit does not exist there. And in 1872 Weierstrass astonished everyone by describing a function that is continuous everywhere, an unbroken line, yet has a corner at every single point, so that it has no derivative anywhere. Mathematicians called such things monsters. The library of the future tells me they are now called fractals and are rather admired.
## Summary

The derivative is the limit of rise over run as the run shrinks to nought: f dash of x equals the limit of, f of x plus h minus f of x, over h. For x squared it gives two x. It is the gradient at every point and the instantaneous rate of change, such as speed. Leibniz wrote d y by d x, Newton a dot, Lagrange f dash. Next, the power rule, which turns all this into a moment's work. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. The first half of the summit asked how fast. The second half asks how much. How much water has flowed into the cistern, if the flow rate keeps changing? How far has a cab travelled, if its speed keeps changing? What is the area under a curved line? These are all one question in different hats, and its answer is the integral.
## The area problem

On the ridge we found areas of rectangles, triangles and circles. But what is the area under a curve, say under the parabola y equals x squared, between x equals nought and x equals one? Picture it: the region bounded below by the x axis, on the right by a vertical line at x equals one, and above by the gently rising curve. It is a curved, horn-shaped piece, thin at the left, rising to a height of one at the right.
## Slices

Here is the idea, which goes back to Archimedes. Cut the region into thin vertical strips, like slicing a loaf. Each strip is almost a rectangle: its width is small, and its height is roughly the height of the curve there. Add up the areas of all the rectangles. That is not exact, because the curve's top is not flat, but it is close. Use thinner strips, and it is closer still.

Let us try. Four strips, each a quarter wide, with heights taken at their right-hand edges: the curve's heights at a quarter, a half, three quarters and one are one sixteenth, four sixteenths, nine sixteenths and sixteen sixteenths. Their total is thirty sixteenths; times the width, a quarter, gives thirty sixty-fourths, about nought point four seven. Too big, since those rectangles poke above the curve.
With ten strips, the total is about nought point three eight five. With a hundred, about nought point three three eight. With a thousand, about nought point three three four.
?? While I pour. Where do you think these totals are heading?
=> Towards one third, nought point three three three and so on.
## The integral
The exact area, the limit of the sums of thinner and thinner slices, is called the integral. Leibniz wrote it like this.

In plain words: the integral from nought to one of x squared d x equals one third. The tall, stretched S is Leibniz's long S, for summa, meaning sum. The x squared is the height of each slice. The d x is the width of each infinitely thin slice. The nought and one at the bottom and top of the S are the limits of integration: where the slicing starts and stops. Read the whole thing as: add up, from nought to one, height times width.
## Archimedes and the parabola

About two hundred and fifty years before Christ, Archimedes found the area of a slice of a parabola, cut off by a straight line: exactly four thirds of a certain triangle drawn inside it. He did it by filling the region with ever smaller triangles, whose areas formed a shrinking geometric sequence: each stage a quarter of the one before. Their sum settles to four thirds. He then proved it rigorously by the method of exhaustion: any other answer, larger or smaller, leads to a contradiction. It was two thousand years ahead of its time.
## Between Archimedes and Leibniz

In 1635 the Italian Bonaventura Cavalieri published a method of indivisibles, thinking of areas as made of infinitely many lines, and volumes of infinitely many planes. Fermat, Pascal, Wallis and others found many areas this way in the following decades. What Newton and Leibniz added was the great discovery that this adding-up is the reverse of differentiation, which is my next lecture but one. That turned dozens of separate clever tricks into a single method.
## Integrals as totals

The integral is not only about areas. If water flows into a cistern at a rate that changes from minute to minute, the total amount is the integral of the rate over time: add up, for each tiny moment, rate times the length of the moment. If a cab's speed changes, the distance travelled is the integral of the speed. On a graph of speed against time, distance is the area under the curve.
?? A cab travels at a steady ten miles an hour for half an hour. What is the area under its speed graph, and what does it mean?
=> A rectangle, ten high and a half wide: area five. Five miles travelled.
## Riemann

In my own century, Bernhard Riemann, in 1854, gave a careful definition of the integral, as exactly this limit of sums of thin rectangles, and showed when it exists. The sums are now called Riemann sums. Riemann was a quiet, shy man, and one of the deepest thinkers of the age; his ideas on curved space later served Einstein, as I read with astonishment in the library of the future.
## Summary

The integral adds up infinitely many infinitely thin slices. Approximate the area under a curve with thin rectangles; as they thin, the total approaches the exact area. The area under x squared from nought to one is one third. Leibniz's long S means sum, and d x is the slice width. Integrals give areas, distances from speeds, and totals from rates. Next, working backwards from derivatives: antiderivatives. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight the view from the summit. The first half of calculus, derivatives, asked how fast. The second half, integrals, asked how much. They looked like two separate peaks. Tonight I shall show you that they are one mountain, seen from two sides. This is the fundamental theorem of calculus, and it is the single most useful fact in all of mathematics.
## A rate and a total

Picture a cistern filling with water. Let the amount of water at time t be A of t. The rate at which water flows in is the derivative of A: how fast the amount is changing. And the total that has flowed in, from the start, is the integral of the rate: the sum, moment by moment, of rate times time. So the integral of the rate gives back the amount. Adding up the rate of change undoes the taking of the rate. That is the whole theorem, in a cistern.
## The area function

Now in pictures. Take a curve, y equals f of x. Define a new function, the area under the curve from some starting point up to x. Call it the area so far. As x moves a little to the right, by a tiny amount d x, how much does the area grow? It gains a thin strip, of height f of x and width d x. So the rate at which the area grows is the height of the curve.
$$ \frac{d}{dx}\int_{a}^{x}f(t)\,dt=f(x)
In plain words: the derivative of the area-so-far function is the original function. Differentiating undoes integrating.
?? While I pour. If the curve is the level line y equals five, how fast does the area under it grow as x moves right?
=> Five square units for each unit of x. The area so far is five x, and its derivative is five.
## The practical form
Here is the form that does all the work. To find the area under f from a to b, you do not need to slice anything. Find any antiderivative, F, a function whose derivative is f. Then:
$$ \int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)
In plain words: the integral from a to b of f equals capital F of b minus capital F of a. The plus c does not matter here, because it is added and subtracted, and cancels.
## The parabola, at last

Two lectures ago, we sliced the area under x squared from nought to one into a thousand strips and crept towards one third. Now: an antiderivative of x squared is x cubed over three. At one, it is one third. At nought, it is nought. One third minus nought: one third. One line instead of a thousand strips.

On paper, mathematicians often put the antiderivative in square brackets with the two limits attached at the right-hand end: a shorthand meaning work out what is inside at the top number, and subtract its value at the bottom number. A brown-paper parcel with a delivery note.
?? Find the area under y equals three x squared from x equals nought to x equals two.
=> An antiderivative is x cubed. At two, eight; at nought, nought. The area is eight.
## Why it was a revolution

Before this theorem, every area or volume was a separate puzzle demanding its own clever trick: Archimedes for the parabola, Cavalieri for some curves, Fermat for others. After it, they became mechanical: find an antiderivative, subtract. Problems that had defeated the ancients became exercises for students. This is what Newton and Leibniz truly gave the world, more than any single result.
## Who found it

Newton's teacher at Cambridge, Isaac Barrow, the first Lucasian Professor, published a geometric version of the relationship in his lectures of 1670, though he did not see its full power. The Scottish mathematician James Gregory had something similar in 1668. Newton and Leibniz each saw it as the central engine and built their calculus around it. Barrow, by the way, resigned his chair in 1669, and Newton succeeded him, aged twenty-six. It is often said that Barrow stood aside to make way for his brilliant pupil; the truth seems to be that he wished to devote himself to divinity, but he certainly admired Newton greatly.
## Distance from speed

A cab's speed after t hours is, let us say, ten plus four t miles an hour, steadily speeding up. How far does it go in the first two hours? An antiderivative of ten plus four t is ten t plus two t squared. At two hours: twenty plus eight, twenty-eight. At nought: nought. Twenty-eight miles. A speedometer reading, integrated, becomes a mileage.
## Summary

The fundamental theorem says differentiation and integration undo each other: the rate of growth of the area under a curve is the height of the curve. So the integral from a to b of f is F of b minus F of a, for any antiderivative F. The area under x squared from nought to one is one third, in a single line. This theorem turned every area problem into routine. Next, definite integrals and areas in more detail. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Most ordinary equations ask: what number makes this true? A differential equation asks something grander: what function makes this true? It describes not a thing but a law of change, and its answer is a whole story through time. Newton, in a Latin anagram hidden in a letter of 1676 meant for Leibniz, said in effect that it is useful to solve differential equations. The modern world is built on them.
## The simplest law

Suppose a quantity grows at a rate proportional to its own size: the bigger it is, the faster it grows. Population, money at compound interest, a chain reaction. Write the quantity as y, depending on time t. The law is:
$$ \frac{dy}{dt}=ky
In plain words: d y by d t equals k times y, where k is a constant measuring how fast. If k is positive, growth; if negative, decay.
The solution is the exponential.

In plain words: y equals y nought times e to the k t, where y nought is the starting amount. Differentiate it and you get k times itself, which is the equation. This is why e is the natural base: it is the function built to obey this law.
?? While I pour. Which simple function is equal to its own derivative?
=> e to the t, or any multiple of it.
## Decay, and the radiocarbon clock

Radioactive atoms decay at a rate proportional to how many remain: k negative. The solution, an exponential decay, halves in a fixed time called the half-life. Carbon fourteen has a half-life of about five thousand seven hundred years, which, the library of the future tells me, lets archaeologists date ancient wood and bone. A decade or two after my day, Marie and Pierre Curie began the study of radioactivity; Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy found the decay law in 1902.
## Newton's law of cooling

Newton proposed in 1701 that a hot body cools at a rate proportional to the difference between its temperature and the room's. A cup of tea at ninety degrees in a room at twenty: the difference, seventy, decays exponentially. The tea cools fast at first, then more and more slowly, creeping towards room temperature but never quite reaching it, in theory. This is why my tea is always too hot, and then, after a single digression on Hamilton, too cold.
## The pendulum and the spring

A weight on a spring is pulled back towards the middle with a force proportional to how far it is displaced. By Newton's second law, its acceleration, the second derivative of position, equals minus a constant times its position.

In plain words: the second derivative of x with respect to t equals minus omega squared times x. The solutions are sine and cosine waves: the spring bobs up and down for ever, in theory. Sine and cosine are the functions whose second derivative is minus themselves, and that is why they describe every vibration: springs, pendulums with small swings, tuning forks, and the air in a concert hall.
?? Differentiate sine t twice. What do you get?
=> First cosine t, then minus sine t: minus the original. Just what the spring equation needs.
## The equations of the world

Fourier described the flow of heat with a differential equation, in 1822. D'Alembert, in 1747, wrote one for the vibrating violin string, whose solutions are waves. And in my own century, James Clerk Maxwell, a Scot whose papers I read with growing amazement by gaslight in Manchester, gathered all of electricity and magnetism into a handful of differential equations, published in their full form in 1865. He found that they predict waves travelling at the speed of light, and concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic wave. Every wireless set and telephone, the library tells me, descends from that calculation.
## Solving them

Some differential equations can be solved with formulas, as we have done. Most cannot. For those, one steps forward in tiny steps: knowing the present value and the rate of change, estimate the value a moment later, and repeat. Euler devised this in the 1760s; it is called Euler's method. It is what Babbage's engines dreamed of doing, and what the electronic computers of the future do, billions of times a second, to forecast tomorrow's weather.
## Summary

A differential equation relates a function to its rates of change, and its solutions are functions. Change in proportion to size gives exponential growth or decay: interest, radiocarbon, cooling tea. The spring equation gives sines and cosines, and so every vibration. Heat, waves, electricity, magnetism and light obey differential equations. Next, infinite series, Taylor's method, and Euler's pi squared over six. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend, and welcome to the summit. Base camp, the foothills and the ridge are behind us. Up here the air is thin, so I shall go slowly, and take a great many cups of tea. Calculus has two halves. The first asks: how fast is something changing? The second asks: how much has built up? Tonight we begin the first, with a question a child could ask: how steep is a curve?
## Straight lines are easy

On the ridge we learnt that the steepness of a straight line, its gradient, is the rise over the run, and it is the same everywhere along the line. A road that climbs one foot in every ten climbs one in ten at the bottom, in the middle, and at the top.
## Curves are not

Now picture the parabola y equals x squared, the smiling U. Walk along it from the bottom to the right. At the very bottom it is level. A little to the right, it rises gently. Further out, steeper and steeper. The steepness changes at every point. So what could we mean by the gradient of the curve at, say, x equals one?
## The tangent

Picture a straight ruler laid against the curve so that it just touches it at one point, without cutting across. That line is called the tangent, from the Latin for touching. Near that point, the tangent and the curve go in the same direction; if you were a very small ant walking on the curve, you would think you were on the tangent. The steepness of the curve at that point is the gradient of its tangent.

The trouble is that a tangent touches at only one point, and to find a gradient we need two points: rise over run. With one point, the rise and the run are both nought, and nought over nought means nothing at all.
## The chord, and creeping closer

Here is the way round, the great idea of the summit. Take two points on the curve, and join them with a straight line called a chord, like a bowstring. Its gradient we can work out. Then move the second point closer to the first, and closer, and watch what happens to the gradient.
On y equals x squared, start at x equals one, where y is one. Take a second point at x equals two, where y is four. The chord rises three over a run of one: gradient three.
Bring the second point to x equals one point five, where y is two point two five. Rise one point two five over a run of nought point five: gradient two point five.
Bring it to x equals one point one, where y is one point two one. Rise nought point two one over nought point one: gradient two point one.
To one point nought one: y is one point nought two nought one. Rise nought point nought two nought one over nought point nought one: gradient two point nought one.
?? While I pour. Can you guess where the gradients three, two point five, two point one, two point nought one are heading?
=> Towards two. The gradient of the curve y equals x squared at x equals one is two.
## What just happened

We never put the two points on top of each other, which would give the meaningless nought over nought. Instead we watched the gradient settle towards a single value as the gap shrank. That settling value is called a limit, and it is the subject of my next lecture. It is exactly what Newton and Leibniz were reaching for, and what Zeno could not quite see.
## Steepness as speed

Steepness has another face: speed. If a graph shows the distance a cab has travelled against time, the gradient is the speed: miles per hour is rise, in miles, over run, in hours. On a straight-line graph, steady speed. On a curve, the speed changes, and the gradient at one moment is the speed at that moment, what the speedometer of a motor car shows, as the library of the future informs me. Newton thought of exactly this: quantities flowing in time, with their rates of flow, which he called fluxions.
?? A stone falls a distance of sixteen times t squared feet in t seconds. Its graph is a parabola. Is its speed steady?
=> No. The graph curves ever more steeply, so the stone goes faster and faster.
## A tool for the summit

So the plan for the summit is this. To find how fast anything is changing at one instant, take a tiny step, find the average rate of change across it, and see what that average settles to as the step shrinks to nothing. This is called differentiation. The result is called the derivative. Next time, limits, carefully. Then derivatives, and rules that make them quick. The tiny step will be called h, and you will come to love h, as I do.
## Summary

A curve's steepness changes from point to point. At a point, it is the gradient of the tangent, the line that just touches there. We estimate it with chords to nearby points and watch the gradient settle as the points come together: on y equals x squared at x equals one, the gradients settle to two. Steepness of a distance graph is speed. Next, limits. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Last time we found the derivative of x squared from first principles: expand, cancel, divide, let h vanish. Splendid, but laborious. Tonight, the reward for that labour: a rule so simple that Mrs Blewitt, hearing it through the door, declared she could have done calculus years ago if only someone had told her.
## The pattern
From first principles, one finds these derivatives.
The derivative of x is one. A line at forty-five degrees has gradient one everywhere.
The derivative of x squared is two x.
The derivative of x cubed is three x squared.
The derivative of x to the four is four x cubed.
Do you see the pattern?
?? While I pour. Guess the derivative of x to the power of five.
=> Five x to the power of four.
## The power rule
$$ \frac{d}{dx}x^{n}=nx^{n-1}
In plain words: the derivative of x to the n is n times x to the n minus one. Bring the power down to the front as a multiplier, and reduce the power by one. Two steps: down, then one less.

Why does it work? For x cubed: x plus h, all cubed, expands to x cubed plus three x squared h plus terms with h squared and h cubed. Take away x cubed, divide by h, and every remaining term but three x squared still contains an h, which vanishes in the limit. The same happens for every power: the binomial expansion, which Newton generalised, always leaves n x to the n minus one.
## Constants and sums
Two more rules, both common sense.

A constant multiplier stays put. If a curve is stretched to five times its height, its gradients are five times as steep. The derivative of five x cubed is five times three x squared, fifteen x squared.
The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Handle each term separately.
A plain constant, such as seven, has derivative nought. The graph y equals seven is a level line, gradient nought everywhere. Things that do not change have no rate of change.
Four x cubed gives twelve x squared. Minus two x squared gives minus four x. Seven x gives seven. Minus nine gives nought.
?? Differentiate three x squared plus five x minus one.
=> Six x plus five.
## Negative and fractional powers
The rule works for any power at all, which is what makes it so mighty. One over x is x to the minus one.
Bring the minus one down, and reduce the power by one, to minus two. So the derivative of one over x is minus one over x squared: always negative, because the curve one over x is always falling.
The square root of x is x to the power of a half. Bring the half down, reduce the power by one, to minus a half.
⟦\frac{d}{dx}\sqrt{x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}⟧
## A practical example

A farmer has a field whose area, in square yards, depends on the length of one side by the formula two x times, fifty minus x, which is a hundred x minus two x squared. How fast does the area change as x grows? The derivative is a hundred minus four x. When x is ten, the area grows by sixty square yards for each extra yard of side. When x is twenty-five, the rate is nought: the area has stopped growing. That, as you will see in two lectures' time, is where the area is greatest.
## Speed and acceleration

Differentiate the distance of a falling stone, sixteen t squared: thirty-two t, the speed. Differentiate again: thirty-two, the acceleration. Differentiating twice gives the second derivative, written d two y by d x squared, which tells how the gradient itself is changing: how fast the speed is changing, or whether a curve bends upwards like a smile or downwards like a frown.
## Summary

The power rule: the derivative of x to the n is n x to the n minus one. Bring the power down, then reduce it by one. Constants multiply through, sums are done term by term, a lone constant gives nought, and the rule works for negative and fractional powers. Differentiating twice gives acceleration and curvature. Next, products and quotients. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. We can now differentiate sums and powers. But real formulas multiply and divide functions: a falling weight times its height, a cost divided by a quantity. Tonight two rules for these, which Leibniz found in the 1670s, and a warning about a tempting mistake.
## The tempting mistake

You might hope that the derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives. Try it on x times x, which is x squared. The derivative of each x is one, and one times one is one. But the derivative of x squared is two x. The hope fails. Leibniz himself, in his early notes, wondered about this and soon saw it was wrong.
## The product rule, with a rectangle

Picture a rectangle, with sides u and v, both slowly growing. Its area is u times v. Now let time tick on a tiny moment. Side u grows by a tiny amount, call it delta u; side v grows by a tiny delta v. How much does the area grow?

The new rectangle is the old one, plus a thin strip along one side, of area u times delta v, plus a thin strip along the other, of area v times delta u, plus a minute corner square, delta u times delta v. That corner is a tiny times a tiny, so small that it vanishes in the limit. So the growth in area is u delta v plus v delta u.
$$ \frac{d}{dx}(uv)=u\frac{dv}{dx}+v\frac{du}{dx}
In plain words: the derivative of u times v is u times the derivative of v, plus v times the derivative of u. Each factor takes its turn to change, while the other holds still.
Check on x squared, as x times x: x times one, plus x times one, is two x. Correct.
?? While I pour. Use the product rule on x squared times x cubed. What do you get?
=> x squared times three x squared, plus x cubed times two x: three x to the four plus two x to the four, five x to the four. The power rule on x to the five agrees.
## A real use

The product rule shines when the factors are different kinds of function, which we shall meet next lecture: x squared times the sine of x, or x times e to the x. Here is a simpler example. A shopkeeper sells n items at a price p, both changing with the season. His takings are n times p. If the price rises by a penny a week while he sells two fewer items a week, the product rule tells him at once whether his takings rise or fall: n times the change in p, plus p times the change in n.
## The quotient rule
For one function divided by another, u over v, there is a companion rule.
$$ \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)=\frac{v\frac{du}{dx}-u\frac{dv}{dx}}{v^{2}}

In plain words: v times the derivative of u, minus u times the derivative of v, all over v squared. The order on top matters, because of the minus sign. The old schoolroom rhyme, which I shall render with dignity: low d high, minus high d low, over the square of what's below.
?? Using the quotient rule, what is the derivative of one over x? Here u is one and v is x.
=> x times nought, minus one times one, over x squared: minus one over x squared. The power rule agrees.
## You can often avoid the quotient rule

A division can be rewritten as a multiplication by a negative power, and then the product rule and the chain rule, which comes next, do the job. Many mathematicians rarely use the quotient rule, preferring to rewrite. Use whichever path you find clearer; the answer is the same, as it must be.
## Leibniz and his differentials

The rectangle argument is essentially Leibniz's own, from his notes of 1675 and 1676, and from his paper of 1684. He treated d of u v as the change in the rectangle, and dropped the corner, d u times d v, as infinitely smaller than the rest. Berkeley would have objected that it is either something or nothing; Cauchy's limits later showed that dropping it is perfectly justified.
## Summary

The derivative of a product is not the product of derivatives. Product rule: u d v by d x plus v d u by d x, as each side of a growing rectangle takes its turn. Quotient rule: v d u minus u d v, over v squared, low d high minus high d low. Rewriting divisions as negative powers often avoids it. Next, the chain rule, for machines inside machines. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. On the ridge, we joined machines end to end: f of g of x, g first, then f. Tonight we ask how fast such a chain changes. The answer, the chain rule, is perhaps the most used rule in all of calculus, and it is as simple as a set of gears.
## Gears

Picture three gear wheels in a row, A, B and C, as in a clock or one of Mr Babbage's engines. Wheel A turns twice for every turn of B. Wheel B turns three times for every turn of C. How many times does A turn for every turn of C? Two times three, six. Rates multiply along a chain.
## The rule
Suppose y depends on u, and u depends on x. Then:
$$ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy}{du}\times\frac{du}{dx}

In plain words: d y by d x equals d y by d u times d u by d x. In Leibniz's notation it looks as if the d u's simply cancel, like fractions. They are not truly fractions, but the notation is so well designed that it leads you to the right answer. This is the sort of thing that made Leibniz's notation win.
## In practice
Take, three x plus one, all to the power of four.

The outside machine raises to the fourth power. The inside machine is three x plus one. Differentiate the outside, keeping the inside untouched in its brown-paper parcel: four times the parcel cubed. Then multiply by the derivative of the inside, which is three.
You could have expanded the bracket to the fourth power and used the power rule, but I should not wish that on anyone, least of all on a Tuesday.
?? While I pour. What is the derivative of, x squared plus one, all squared?
=> Outside: two times the parcel. Inside derivative: two x. So two times, x squared plus one, times two x, which is four x times, x squared plus one.
## A rhyme for the chain
Outside first, leave the inside be; then times the inside's derivative, and you are free. It scans poorly, I admit, but Euclid the cat has heard it so often that he purrs at the word derivative.
## Square roots

The square root of, one plus x squared, is the parcel to the power of a half. Outside: a half times the parcel to the minus a half. Inside derivative: two x. Multiply: x over the square root of, one plus x squared.
## Rates in the world

The chain rule describes how rates pass along real chains. A balloon is being inflated. Its radius grows at one inch per second. How fast is its volume growing, when the radius is ten inches? The volume is four thirds pi r cubed, so d V by d r is four pi r squared. Then d V by d t is d V by d r times d r by d t: four pi times a hundred, times one, about twelve hundred and fifty-seven cubic inches per second. The bigger the balloon, the faster the air must go in to keep the radius growing steadily, which every child with a balloon has discovered by experiment.
?? A square's side grows at two centimetres per second. How fast is its area growing when the side is five?
=> Area is s squared, so d A by d s is two s, which is ten. Times two centimetres per second: twenty square centimetres per second.
## The chain rule inside your slate

The library of the future tells me that the machines that learn to recognise speech and pictures are trained by a method that is, at heart, the chain rule applied over and over through millions of connected stages. Leibniz, who built a calculating machine and dreamed of a calculus of reasoning, would have been delighted.
## Summary

For a function of a function, d y by d x equals d y by d u times d u by d x. Differentiate the outside, leaving the inside in its parcel, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. Rates multiply along a chain like gears. Next, the great practical use of derivatives: finding the highest and lowest points. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight the derivative earns its living. Nearly every practical question that begins with the words most or least, the largest field, the cheapest tin, the quickest path, is answered by one simple observation. Pierre de Fermat made it around 1636, before Newton or Leibniz were even born.
## The observation

Walk along a smooth hill. As you climb, the ground slopes up. As you descend, it slopes down. At the very top, for one instant, it is level. The same at the bottom of a valley. So at a smooth highest or lowest point, the gradient is nought.
$$ \frac{dy}{dx}=0
These points are called stationary points, or turning points: maxima for peaks, minima for valleys.
## The method
Three steps. Differentiate. Set the derivative equal to nought. Solve the equation.

Differentiate: two x minus six. Set to nought: two x minus six equals nought, so x is three. At x equals three, y is nine minus eighteen plus ten, one. The lowest point is at three, one. On the ridge we would have completed the square to find this; now one line of calculus does it.
?? While I pour. Find where y equals ten x minus x squared has its turning point.
=> The derivative is ten minus two x, which is nought when x is five. And y is fifty minus twenty-five, twenty-five.
## Peak or valley?

How do we know which kind? Look at the second derivative, the rate at which the gradient changes. At a valley, the gradient goes from negative to nought to positive: it is increasing, so the second derivative is positive. The curve smiles. At a peak, the gradient goes from positive to nought to negative: decreasing, second derivative negative. The curve frowns.
For y equals ten x minus x squared, the second derivative is minus two: negative, a peak. A maximum.

Occasionally the second derivative is nought too, and we must look more carefully; y equals x cubed is level at the origin but is neither peak nor valley, merely pausing on its way up, like a staircase landing.
## The farmer's field

A farmer has a hundred yards of fencing and wants to enclose the largest rectangular field against a long straight wall, so the wall forms one side. If the two sides at right angles to the wall are x yards each, the side parallel to the wall is a hundred minus two x. The area is:

Differentiate: a hundred minus four x. Set to nought: x is twenty-five. The field is twenty-five yards deep and fifty long, area twelve hundred and fifty square yards. The second derivative, minus four, confirms a maximum. That is the field we met in the lecture on the power rule.
## The cheapest tin

A tinsmith must make a cylindrical tin holding a fixed volume, using the least metal. Too tall and thin wastes metal on the sides; too short and wide wastes it on the lid and base. Calculus shows that the least metal is used when the height equals the diameter. Next time you are in the larder, look at a tin of peas; many tins are taller than this, for reasons of stacking, labelling and the hands that hold them. Mrs Blewitt says that is because tinsmiths have never been consulted by a housekeeper.
?? Two positive numbers add to twenty. What is the largest their product can be?
=> Call them x and twenty minus x. The product is twenty x minus x squared; its derivative, twenty minus two x, is nought when x is ten. Ten times ten, a hundred.
## Nature's economy

Nature, too, seems to find extremes. Light travelling from air into water bends, and Fermat showed, around 1662, that the path it takes is the one of least time. A soap film stretched on a wire frame takes the shape of least area. A hanging chain settles to the shape of least energy. Mathematicians of the eighteenth century, Euler foremost, built a whole subject, the calculus of variations, from such questions. The brachistochrone problem, the curve of quickest descent, was posed by Johann Bernoulli in 1696; Newton, so the story goes, received it one afternoon and sent his anonymous solution the next morning, and Bernoulli said he recognised the lion by his claw. That much is well attested in the letters of the time.
## Summary

At a smooth maximum or minimum the derivative is nought. Differentiate, set to nought, solve. The second derivative tells peak from valley: negative for a peak, positive for a valley. The method finds the largest field, the cheapest tin, the best price, and nature's own shortest paths. Next, derivatives of the great functions: e to the x, logarithms, sine and cosine. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. On the ridge we met the exponential, the logarithm and the wave. Tonight we discover their derivatives, and the reasons, at last, why mathematicians insist on the curious number e and on measuring angles in radians. Both choices make the calculus beautifully simple.
## The function that is its own derivative

Recall the exponential curve, rising ever more steeply. Its steepness at any point is proportional to its height. For two to the x, the gradient is about nought point six nine times the height. For three to the x, about one point one times the height. Somewhere between two and three there must be a base for which the gradient is exactly equal to the height. That base is e, about two point seven one eight.
$$ \frac{d}{dx}e^{x}=e^{x}

In plain words: the derivative of e to the x is e to the x itself. The function is its own rate of change. Wherever you stand on the curve, the slope is the height. This is the deepest reason e is called natural: it describes anything whose rate of growth equals its size, such as money compounding continually, or a population with plenty of food.
With the chain rule, the derivative of e to the k x is k times e to the k x.
?? While I pour. What is the derivative of e to the power of minus x?
=> Minus e to the minus x. The chain rule brings down the minus one. A decay curve, falling at a rate equal to its height.
## The natural logarithm
The natural logarithm, l n of x, undoes e to the x. Its derivative is wonderfully simple.
$$ \frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac{1}{x}

In plain words: the derivative of the natural log of x is one over x. At x equals one the log curve climbs at gradient one; at x equals ten, it creeps up at a tenth; at a thousand, a thousandth. It grows for ever, but ever more slowly, like a reputation built on a single good book.
This also fills a gap. The power rule could produce x to every power except minus one: nothing differentiates to x to the minus one by the power rule. The logarithm is the missing piece.
## Sine and cosine

Picture the spot on the turning wheel again. As it passes the far right, rising, its height is changing fastest: the sine wave is steepest as it crosses nought. At the top, the height momentarily stops changing: the sine wave is level at its peak. The rate of change of the sine wave is itself a wave, but shifted: it is the cosine.
$$ \frac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x
$$ \frac{d}{dx}\cos x=-\sin x

In plain words: the derivative of sine is cosine, and the derivative of cosine is minus sine. Differentiate four times and you are back where you started: sine, cosine, minus sine, minus cosine, sine. A merry-go-round.

But these neat results hold only when angles are measured in radians. In degrees, every derivative would carry an awkward factor of pi over a hundred and eighty. This is why mathematicians, and I, insist on radians at the summit. The Babylonians are not to blame; they had no calculus.
?? What is the derivative of sine of two x?
=> By the chain rule: cosine of two x, times two. Two cosine two x.
## Springs and pendulums

Here is a wonder. Differentiate sine twice and you get minus sine: the second derivative is minus the original. A weight on a spring is pulled back with a force proportional to how far it is stretched, in the opposite direction. Its acceleration, the second derivative of its position, is minus a constant times its position. So its motion must be a sine wave. That is why springs, pendulums, tuning forks and violin strings all vibrate in sine waves. Calculus explains Fourier's waves.
## Euler's surprise

Leonhard Euler, in his Introduction to Analysis of the Infinite of 1748, showed that e to the x and the sine and cosine waves are close relatives, once the square root of minus one is allowed in. That leads, by a short step, to the famous equation e to the i pi plus one equals nought, which links five of the most important numbers in mathematics. It is often called Euler's identity, though he does not seem to have written it in exactly that form himself. I shall say more of Euler next time.
## Summary

The derivative of e to the x is e to the x; of the natural log of x, one over x; of sine, cosine; of cosine, minus sine, with angles in radians. Combined with the chain, product and quotient rules, these differentiate almost any formula you are likely to meet. They explain growth, decay and vibration. Next, the life of the most prolific mathematician in history, Leonhard Euler. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. On the ridge we learnt that many machines can be run backwards: subtraction undoes addition, logarithms undo powers. Tonight we run the derivative machine backwards. Given a rate of change, what was the original function? This backwards operation is called finding an antiderivative, and next time you will see why it is the key to every integral.
## The question
The derivative of x squared is two x. So, running backwards: what function has derivative two x? x squared. We say x squared is an antiderivative of two x.

But it is not the only one. x squared plus five also has derivative two x, since the derivative of five is nought. So does x squared minus a hundred. Any constant can be added, because constants vanish when you differentiate. So we write:
$$ \int 2x\,dx=x^{2}+c

In plain words: the integral of two x d x is x squared plus c, where c stands for any constant. This is called an indefinite integral: an integral sign with no limits, meaning the antiderivative. The plus c is called the constant of integration. Forgetting it is the commonest slip at the summit; I have watched Senior Wranglers do it, and Fourteenth Wranglers, I confess, more than once.
?? While I pour. What function has derivative three x squared?
=> x cubed, plus any constant.
## The power rule backwards
The power rule said: bring the power down, then reduce it by one. Backwards: raise the power by one, then divide by the new power.
$$ \int x^{n}\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+c

In plain words: the integral of x to the n is x to the n plus one, over n plus one, plus c. Check by differentiating: bring down n plus one, reduce the power to n, and the n plus one cancels. Splendid.

So the integral of x squared is x cubed over three. The integral of x to the four is x to the five over five. The integral of a constant, say seven, is seven x, since seven is seven times x to the nought.
?? What is the integral of x to the five?
=> x to the six over six, plus c.
## One exception

The rule fails for n equals minus one: it would give x to the nought over nought, which is nonsense. Here the logarithm steps in, as we found two lectures ago: the derivative of the natural log of x is one over x.
⟦\int\frac{1}{x}\,dx=\ln x+c⟧
For positive x, the integral of one over x is the natural log of x, plus c.
## The other great functions
Each derivative we know gives an antiderivative for free, read backwards.
The integral of e to the x is e to the x, plus c: still its own.
The integral of cosine x is sine x, plus c.
The integral of sine x is minus cosine x, plus c. The minus sign is there because the derivative of cosine is minus sine.
## Sums and constants
As with derivatives, take sums term by term, and let constant multipliers stand outside.

Six x squared gives six times x cubed over three, two x cubed. Four x gives four times x squared over two, two x squared. Minus five gives minus five x. One constant at the end mops up all the others.
## Finding the c

Sometimes we know one value, which pins down c. A stone is dropped, and its speed after t seconds is thirty-two t feet per second. How far has it fallen? The antiderivative of thirty-two t is sixteen t squared plus c. At the start, t equals nought, it has fallen nought, so c is nought. Distance: sixteen t squared, Galileo's law, recovered by running the derivative backwards.
## Harder cases

Differentiation is mechanical: any formula built from the usual functions can be differentiated by the rules. Antidifferentiation is an art. Some functions have antiderivatives that cannot be written with the usual functions at all. The bell curve's e to the minus x squared is the famous example; its integral had to be given a name of its own and tabulated. So mathematicians gathered tricks, which fill whole books: substitution, integration by parts, and many more. I shall show you substitution in a later lecture.
## Summary

An antiderivative undoes differentiation. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power; for one over x, use the natural log. e to the x stays e to the x; cosine gives sine; sine gives minus cosine. Always add plus c, and find c from a known value if one is given. Next, the great bridge between the two halves of the summit: the fundamental theorem. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Last time the fundamental theorem gave us a quick way to find areas. Tonight we look at what happens when the curve dips below the axis, how to find the area between two curves, and how Archimedes' sphere can be recovered by spinning a curve like a potter's wheel.
## Above and below
A definite integral counts area above the x axis as positive and area below as negative. The slices below the axis have negative heights, so height times width is negative.
Consider one complete wave of sine x, from nought to two pi. The first half arches above the axis, the second half dips below by exactly the same amount.

The integral is nought: the positive and negative areas cancel. If you want the total area, regardless of sign, integrate each half separately and add their sizes. The first arch alone, from nought to pi, has area two.
?? While I pour. Using the antiderivative minus cosine x, check that the integral of sine x from nought to pi is two.
=> Minus cosine of pi is minus minus one, plus one. Minus cosine of nought is minus one. One minus, minus one, is two.
## In a sense this is a feature

Signed area is often exactly what we want. If speed can be negative, meaning travel backwards, the integral of speed gives the net change in position: how far from the starting point you end up, not how far you walked. A cab that drives five miles out and five miles back has a net integral of nought, though the driver would charge for ten.
## Area between two curves
Picture two curves, one above the other between two points where they cross. The area between them is found by slicing vertically: each slice has height equal to the top curve minus the bottom curve.
$$ \int_{a}^{b}\left(f(x)-g(x)\right)dx
In plain words: the integral from a to b of the top function minus the bottom function.

Example: the line y equals x and the parabola y equals x squared cross at nought and at one. Between them, the line is on top. The area is the integral of x minus x squared from nought to one: an antiderivative is x squared over two minus x cubed over three. At one, a half minus a third, one sixth. At nought, nought. The area is one sixth.
?? Between nought and one, which is higher: y equals x, or y equals x squared? Try x equals a half.
=> x is a half, x squared a quarter. The line is higher.
## Volumes by spinning

Now take a curve and spin it around the x axis, like clay on a potter's wheel. It sweeps out a solid. Slice that solid perpendicular to the axis: each slice is a thin disc, a coin, with radius equal to the height of the curve, y, and thickness d x. Its volume is pi y squared d x. Add them up.
## Archimedes' sphere

Spin a semicircle of radius r, whose curve is y squared equals r squared minus x squared, from x equals minus r to r. The volume is the integral of pi times, r squared minus x squared. An antiderivative is pi times, r squared x minus x cubed over three. Work out the values at r and minus r and subtract, and you get four thirds pi r cubed. Archimedes' sphere, the one carved on his tomb, recovered in four lines. Archimedes needed a lifetime of genius; we need the fundamental theorem and a cup of tea. That is not because we are cleverer, my dear friend, but because we stand on his shoulders, and Newton's, and Leibniz's.
## A cone, too

Spin the straight line y equals x, from nought to h, and you get a cone of height h and radius h. Its volume is the integral of pi x squared from nought to h, which is pi h cubed over three: one third of the matching cylinder, pi h squared times h. The mysterious one third of the cone, which we met in the geometry lectures, now has its reason: it is the one third that comes from integrating x squared.
## Summary

Definite integrals count area below the axis as negative, so a full sine wave integrates to nought. The area between curves is the integral of top minus bottom. Spinning a curve makes a solid whose volume is the integral of pi y squared d x, which gives the sphere and the cone with their famous fractions. Next, the integrator's chief trick: substitution. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Integration, I warned you, is an art rather than a machine. Tonight I teach you its chief trick. Differentiation had the chain rule for functions inside functions, the parcel inside a parcel. Integration has the chain rule run backwards, which is called substitution. It is a little like recognising a friend in disguise.
## A reminder of the chain rule
To differentiate sine of x squared: the outer function is sine, the inner is x squared. Derivative of the outer, cosine of x squared, times derivative of the inner, two x. So:
⟦\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x^{2})=2x\cos(x^{2})⟧

Reading backwards: the integral of two x times cosine of x squared is sine of x squared, plus c. The telltale sign is that the inner part, x squared, appears inside the cosine, and its derivative, two x, appears outside as a multiplier. When you see a parcel inside a parcel and the derivative of the inner parcel lying alongside, think substitution.
## The method
First: choose the inner part and call it u. Here, u equals x squared.
Second: find d u. Since the derivative of u is two x, we write d u equals two x d x. This is Leibniz's notation at its most cunning: we treat d u and d x almost as numbers, and it works.
Third: rewrite the integral entirely in u. Two x d x becomes d u; cosine of x squared becomes cosine of u.
$$ \int 2x\cos(x^{2})\,dx=\int\cos u\,du
Fourth: integrate. The integral of cosine u is sine u, plus c.
Fifth: put the original back. Sine of x squared, plus c.
?? While I pour. Why did we choose u to be x squared, rather than two x?
=> Because x squared is the inner part, and its derivative, two x, is already sitting outside, ready to become d u.
## A second example

Integrate three x squared times, x cubed plus one, all to the power of four. Let u be x cubed plus one, the inner part. Then d u is three x squared d x, which is exactly the rest. The integral becomes the integral of u to the four, which is u to the five over five. Put back: x cubed plus one, to the power five, all over five, plus c.
?? Check by differentiating x cubed plus one, to the five, over five, using the chain rule.
=> Bring down five: five over five is one, times x cubed plus one to the four, times the inner derivative three x squared. We get back the original.
## When a constant is missing

Sometimes the derivative is present except for a constant. To integrate x times e to the x squared: let u be x squared, so d u is two x d x, and x d x is half of d u. The integral becomes a half times the integral of e to the u, which is a half e to the u. Put back: a half e to the x squared, plus c. Constants can be fixed; missing x's cannot. If the problem were e to the x squared alone, with no x outside, substitution would not help, and indeed, as I mentioned, that integral has no formula among the usual functions.
## Logarithms appear

Integrate two x over, x squared plus one. Let u be x squared plus one; d u is two x d x. The integral becomes one over u, d u, which is the natural log of u. So the answer is the natural log of, x squared plus one, plus c. Whenever the top is the derivative of the bottom, the answer is the log of the bottom. This pattern is worth remembering like a friend's face.
## Other tricks of the trade

There are other methods. Integration by parts reverses the product rule. Partial fractions split complicated fractions into simple ones. Trigonometric substitutions turn square roots into sines. In my day there were enormous tables of integrals, and students learned to recognise their forms as a naturalist learns birds. Today, the library of the future informs me, machines do most of it. But the art of recognising structure remains: it is what lets you see what a formula means.
## Summary

Substitution reverses the chain rule. Spot an inner part whose derivative appears as a multiplier; call it u, write d u in terms of d x, rewrite and integrate in u, then put x back. Constants can be adjusted; missing variables cannot. When the top is the derivative of the bottom, the answer is the log of the bottom. Next, putting calculus to work on motion: falling stones and flying cannonballs. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Newton invented his fluxions to describe motion: the moon in its orbit, the apple in its fall. Tonight we use our completed calculus to describe the motion of a cricket ball, a cannonball and a cab. It is the calculus doing the work it was born for.
## The chain of three

Position tells you where something is. Velocity tells you how fast its position is changing, and in which direction. Acceleration tells you how fast its velocity is changing. Each is the derivative of the one before.
⟦v=\frac{ds}{dt},\quad a=\frac{dv}{dt}⟧

In plain words: velocity is d s by d t, the rate of change of position s with time t. Acceleration is d v by d t. And going the other way, integrating acceleration gives velocity, and integrating velocity gives position.
## Galileo's law, derived

Near the Earth, ignoring air, a falling body has constant acceleration, which we call g: about nine point eight metres per second per second, or thirty-two feet per second per second. For easy sums, let us call it ten.
Integrate the acceleration, ten, to get velocity: ten t plus c. If the stone is dropped from rest, the velocity at t equals nought is nought, so c is nought. Velocity: ten t.
Integrate again to get distance fallen: five t squared plus another constant, also nought, since it starts with no distance fallen.
?? While I pour. Using five t squared, how far does a stone fall in three seconds?
=> Five times nine: forty-five metres.

Galileo found by experiment, rolling balls down ramps and timing them with a water clock, that the distance grows as the square of the time. We have derived his law from a single assumption: constant acceleration.
## Throwing upwards

Throw a cricket ball straight up at twenty metres per second. Now gravity opposes its motion, so its acceleration is minus ten. Integrate: velocity is twenty minus ten t, using the starting speed for the constant. Integrate again: height is twenty t minus five t squared.

When is it highest? At the top, it stops for an instant before falling, so the velocity is nought. Twenty minus ten t equals nought gives t equals two seconds. Its height then: forty minus twenty, twenty metres. When does it land? When the height is nought again: twenty t minus five t squared equals nought, so t equals nought or four. It lands after four seconds: two up, two down, exactly symmetrical.
?? What is the ball's velocity when it lands, at four seconds?
=> Twenty minus forty, minus twenty metres per second: the same speed it was thrown with, now heading down.
## Cannonballs

Fire a cannonball at an angle. Its sideways motion has no acceleration, ignoring air, so it moves sideways at a steady speed. Its upward motion is exactly like the cricket ball. Put them together and its path is a parabola, as Galileo showed in 1638. And by calculus one finds that, ignoring air, the greatest range comes from firing at forty-five degrees. Real gunners, troubled by air resistance, found somewhat lower angles better; the calculus of air resistance is much harder, and occupied mathematicians for centuries.
## Newton's second law

Newton's second law says force equals mass times acceleration. Since acceleration is the second derivative of position, this is an equation about rates of change of rates of change. Knowing the forces, you find the acceleration; integrating twice, you find the motion. That is how Newton calculated the orbits of the planets, and it is how, in 1846, Adams in Cambridge and Le Verrier in Paris each predicted, from small wobbles in the orbit of Uranus, the existence and position of a new planet, Neptune, which was found within a degree of Le Verrier's prediction. The planet was discovered with pen and paper before it was seen. I was a schoolboy of seventeen in Bristol at the time, and I remember reading of it in the newspaper, and the bad feeling between the English and the French over who deserved the credit.
## The cab, once more

A cab's velocity is the derivative of its position; the meter integrates its speed to charge for distance. If it brakes from ten metres per second at two metres per second per second, its velocity is ten minus two t; it stops after five seconds, having travelled ten t minus t squared, which at five is twenty-five metres. That is the stopping distance, which engineers in the future compute for every motor-car.
## Summary

Velocity is the derivative of position; acceleration is the derivative of velocity. Integrate acceleration twice, using starting values for the constants, to find the motion. A dropped stone falls five t squared metres, roughly; a ball thrown up at twenty metres per second peaks after two seconds at twenty metres. Newton's second law turns forces into motion, and found Neptune. Next, equations about rates of change themselves: differential equations. Good night, my dear friend.

## Sums that settle, and sums that do not

A half, plus a quarter, plus an eighth, and so on for ever: the running totals are a half, three quarters, seven eighths, creeping towards one. We say the series converges to one. The running totals are called partial sums, and the series converges if they settle on a limit.
But shrinking terms are not enough. Consider one, plus a half, plus a third, plus a quarter, and so on: the harmonic series.

Its terms shrink towards nought, yet its total grows without limit. Around 1350, the French scholar Nicole Oresme proved it with a lovely trick. Group the terms: a third and a quarter together are more than a half. The next four, a fifth to an eighth, are more than a half. The next eight are more than a half. You can collect halves for ever, so the total passes any number you name. It grows very slowly: you need more than twelve thousand terms to pass ten. But it never stops.
?? While I pour. A fifth, a sixth, a seventh and an eighth: why is their sum more than a half?
=> Each is at least an eighth, and there are four of them, so together they are at least four eighths, a half. In fact more.
## Pi from odd numbers
Now a sum with a surprise in it. One, minus a third, plus a fifth, minus a seventh, and so on, alternating.

The total is pi over four. Leibniz published it in 1682, and was delighted. It is called Leibniz's series. But the library of the future tells me that the Indian mathematician Madhava of Sangamagrama, in Kerala, had found it, along with series for sine and cosine, around the year 1400, nearly three centuries earlier. His school's work did not reach Europe. The odd numbers, it seems, know about circles, and they told an Indian astronomer first.
## Taylor's recipe

In 1715 Brook Taylor published the following idea. Suppose a smooth function can be written as a long polynomial: a constant, plus something times x, plus something times x squared, and so on for ever. How do we find the coefficients? Use derivatives at nought. The constant is the function's value at nought. The coefficient of x is its first derivative there. The coefficient of x squared is the second derivative divided by two. In general, the n th derivative, divided by n factorial. Factorial, you will recall, means multiplying down: four factorial is four times three times two times one, twenty-four.
## e to the x
Apply the recipe to e to the x. Every derivative of e to the x is e to the x, and at nought every one equals one. So every coefficient is one over a factorial.

Put x equals one, and you have a recipe for e itself: one, plus one, plus a half, plus a sixth, plus a twenty-fourth, and so on. Those first five terms already give two point seven oh eight. The true value is two point seven one eight. Factorials grow so fast that the terms vanish at a gallop.
?? Add one, plus one, plus a half. Then add a sixth. Roughly what do you have?
=> Two and a half, then about two point six six seven. Getting close to e.
## Sine and cosine

The same recipe gives sine: x, minus x cubed over three factorial, plus x to the five over five factorial, and so on, alternating. This is how calculating machines, and your little glass slate, actually compute sines: by adding a few terms of a series. When Babbage designed his engines to compute tables, it was series and differences he planned to crank through. The recipe is often called a Maclaurin series when centred at nought, after the Scot Colin Maclaurin, who used it widely in 1742.
## Euler's crowning trick

And now the Basel problem, as I promised when we spoke of Euler. Euler took the series for sine x over x: one minus x squared over three factorial, plus x to the four over five factorial, and so on. He knew this function is nought at x equals pi, two pi, three pi and so on, and at minus those. A polynomial can be written as a product of factors, one for each root. Daringly, he treated this infinite series as an infinite polynomial, and wrote it as a product: one minus x squared over pi squared, times one minus x squared over four pi squared, and so on. Multiply out and compare the coefficient of x squared on each side. On one side, minus one sixth. On the other, minus one over pi squared, times one plus a quarter plus a ninth and so on. Set them equal, and out falls the answer.
It was not rigorous: treating an infinite series as a polynomial needed justification, which Euler and later Weierstrass supplied. But it was right, and it was magnificent.
## Summary

An infinite series converges if its partial sums settle. The harmonic series diverges, as Oresme showed by collecting halves. One minus a third plus a fifth gives pi over four, found by Madhava and later Leibniz. Taylor's recipe builds functions from their derivatives: e to the x is the sum of x to the n over n factorial. Euler used the sine series to show the sum of reciprocal squares is pi squared over six. Next, three great characters of my own day: Hamilton, Cayley and Sylvester. Good night, my dear friend.

## Two branches

Calculus is the mathematics of continuous change. It has two branches. Differential calculus studies rates of change: how fast something is changing at an instant, or how steep a curve is at a point. Its central idea is the derivative. Integral calculus studies accumulation: totals built up from tiny pieces, such as areas under curves or distances from speeds. Its central idea is the integral.
## The bridge

The two branches are joined by the fundamental theorem of calculus, which says that differentiation and integration undo each other. That turns hard problems about areas into easier ones about derivatives, and is the engine of the whole subject.
?? While I pour. If a cab's speed is known at every moment, which branch tells you how far it travelled?
=> Integral calculus. Adding up speed times each tiny piece of time gives the distance.
## Before Newton and Leibniz

Ideas of calculus are old. Archimedes found areas and volumes by summing thin slices, in the method of exhaustion. Indian mathematicians of the Kerala school found infinite series for sine and cosine around 1400. In the seventeenth century, Cavalieri, Fermat, Wallis, Barrow and others found tangents and areas by ingenious methods.
## Newton and Leibniz

Isaac Newton, in the 1660s, developed his method of fluxions, and used it in his Principia of 1687 to explain the motion of the planets. Gottfried Leibniz, independently, developed calculus in the 1670s and published first, in 1684. His notation, d y by d x and the long S for integrals, is the one we use. A bitter dispute over priority followed, with accusations of plagiarism; it is now accepted that both discovered calculus independently.
## Foundations

Early calculus used infinitely small quantities, infinitesimals, which were hard to justify. In 1734 Bishop George Berkeley mocked them as the ghosts of departed quantities. In the nineteenth century, Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Karl Weierstrass rebuilt calculus on limits, defined without any talk of the infinitely small, and Riemann made the integral precise. In the twentieth century, Abraham Robinson showed, in 1960, that infinitesimals could after all be made rigorous, in what is called non-standard analysis.
## What it does

Calculus is used everywhere: in physics, for motion, electricity, heat and waves; in engineering, for structures and machines; in economics, for marginal cost and growth; in biology, for populations and the spread of disease; in medicine, for doses and rates. Differential equations, built from derivatives, are the language of the laws of nature. Our own lectures at the summit gave you its main tools: limits, derivatives, integrals and series.
## Summary

Calculus studies continuous change: derivatives for rates, integrals for totals, joined by the fundamental theorem. Its roots go back to Archimedes; Newton and Leibniz created it independently; Cauchy and Weierstrass made it rigorous with limits. It is the mathematical language of science.

## History

According to Hankel (1871), the modern concept of limit originates from Proposition X.1 of Euclid's Elements, which forms the basis of the Method of exhaustion found in Euclid and Archimedes: "Two unequal magnitudes being set out, if from the greater there is subtracted a magnitude greater than its half, and from that which is left a magnitude greater than its half, and if this process is repeated continually, then there will be left some magnitude less than the lesser magnitude set out."

Grégoire de Saint-Vincent gave the first definition of limit (terminus) of a geometric series in his work Opus Geometricum (1647): "The terminus of a progression is the end of the series, which none progression can reach, even not if she is continued in infinity, but which she can approach nearer than a given segment."

In the Scholium to Principia in 1687, Isaac Newton had a clear definition of a limit, stating that "Those ultimate ratios... are not actually ratios of ultimate quantities, but limits... which they can approach so closely that their difference is less than any given quantity". Bruce Pourciau further argues that, in addition to Newton actually having a more sophisticated understanding of limits than he is generally credited with, he also provided the first epsilon argument.

The modern definition of a limit goes back to Bernard Bolzano who, in 1817, developed the basics of the epsilon-delta technique to define continuous functions. However, his work remained unknown to other mathematicians until thirty years after his death.
Augustin-Louis Cauchy in 1821, followed by Karl Weierstrass, formalized the definition of the limit of a function which became known as the (epsilon, delta)-definition of limit.
The modern notation of placing the arrow below the limit symbol was invented by John Gaston Leathem in 1905 and popularized by G. H. Hardy's 1908 textbook A Course of Pure Mathematics.

This section deals with the idea of limits of sequences of functions, not to be confused with the idea of limits of functions, discussed below.

## Nonstandard analysis

In non-standard analysis (which involves a hyperreal enlargement of the number system), the limit of a sequence ⟦( a_{n} )⟧ can be expressed as the standard part of the value ⟦a_{H}⟧ of the natural extension of the sequence at an infinite hypernatural index ⟦n = H⟧. Thus,
$$ \lim_{n → ∞} a_{n} = \operatorname{st} ( a_{H} )
In plain words: it says that the two sides are equal. It uses a named function, such as sine, cosine or log, which turns one number into another.

Here, the standard part function "st" rounds off each finite hyperreal number to the nearest real number (the difference between them is infinitesimal). This formalizes the natural intuition that for "very large" values of the index, the terms in the sequence are "very close" to the limit value of the sequence. Conversely, the standard part of a hyperreal ⟦a = [ a_{n} ]⟧ represented in the ultrapower construction by a Cauchy sequence ⟦( a_{n} )⟧, is simply the limit of that sequence:
$$ \operatorname{st} ( a ) = \lim_{n → ∞} a_{n}
In this sense, taking the limit and taking the standard part are equivalent procedures.
## Limit set of a sequence

Let ⟦\{ a_{n} \}_{n > 0}⟧ be a sequence in a topological space ⟦X⟧. For concreteness, ⟦X⟧ can be thought of as ⟦ℝ⟧, but the definitions hold more generally. The limit set is the set of points such that if there is a convergent subsequence ⟦\{ a_{n_{k}} \}_{k > 0}⟧ with ⟦a_{n_{k}} → a⟧, then ⟦a⟧ belongs to the limit set. In this context, such an ⟦a⟧ is sometimes called a limit point.

A use of this notion is to characterize the "long-term behavior" of oscillatory sequences. For example, consider the sequence ⟦a_{n} = ( − 1 )^{n}⟧. Starting from n=1, the first few terms of this sequence are ⟦− 1 , + 1 , − 1 , + 1 , ⋯⟧. It can be checked that it is oscillatory, so has no limit, but it has two limit points ⟦\{ − 1 , + 1 \}⟧.

To any sequence of increasing times ⟦\{ t_{n} \}⟧, there is an associated sequence of positions ⟦\{ x_{n} \} = \{ γ ( t_{n} ) \}⟧. If ⟦x⟧ is the limit set of the sequence ⟦\{ x_{n} \}⟧ for any sequence of increasing times, then ⟦x⟧ is a limit set of the trajectory.
Technically, this is the ⟦ω⟧-limit set. The corresponding limit set for sequences of decreasing time is called the ⟦α⟧-limit set.
